metadata.note: Version 4 adds H-diamond-proxy-11 (storage key aliasing: dual-role hook collapses token-hook swap fees and pool/liquidity-hook fees into same tokensOwed slot, enabling double-claim). Version 3 adds H-diamond-proxy-08/09/10 (flag non-overlap reentrancy class). Version 2 note: Prior H-DP-01 (operator precedence deposit0|deposit1==0) confirmed FALSE POSITIVE — Solidity '|' (precedence 9) binds tighter than '==' (precedence 11), making the parse (deposit0|deposit1)==0 which is correct. All prior hypotheses derived from mechanism analysis of TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags, fee storage key construction, and queue execution ordering. New hypotheses (v3) derived from bitwise flag overlap analysis across guard flag constants. H-11 derived from coupled state mapping (_storeHookFees HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG branch vs _storeNonTokenHookFees) identifying identical key formula when hook==tokenHook and tokenFee==tokenFor.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy window: SWAP_GUARD_FLAG cleared mid-swap during queued fee execution
hypotheses.summary: _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers (AMMModule.sol ~line 3190) calls _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) before iterating the transfer loop. This clears SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (and all custom execution flags) while the ENTERED bit remains set. External protocols that guard oracle reads or price-sensitive logic with checkAMMExecutionState(SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) will see 'not in swap' during active swap finalization. ERC777 token callbacks or safeTransfer recipients can observe and exploit this false state.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker uses an ERC777 token as hook fee currency in a pool. 2. A swap through the pool accumulates hook fees; collectHookFeesByHook is called by the hook during the swap, routing to the queue (SWAP_GUARD_FLAG set). 3. Swap reaches _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse (~line 2246-2248), which self-calls executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers. 4. Inside _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers, _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) fires (~line 3190): SWAP_GUARD_FLAG is cleared, ENTERED remains. 5. safeTransfer of the ERC777 fee to the hook triggers tokensReceived on the hook contract. 6. Inside tokensReceived, attacker calls an external lending protocol or AMM oracle that invokes checkAMMExecutionState(SWAP_GUARD_FLAG). 7. The view returns false — oracle accepts the read as 'no active swap.' 8. Attacker borrows against the manipulated price in the same transaction.
hypotheses.victim: External protocols (lending markets, MEV bots, price oracles) that integrate with the AMM and call checkAMMExecutionState(SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) to guard against read-only reentrancy. They observe incorrect execution state during active swap finalization.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker exploits the oracle that accepted a price read during the false 'no-swap' window. With the AMM mid-swap (reserves partially updated), spot price may be temporarily skewed. Attacker can borrow against the inflated collateral or execute sandwich trades that reference the stale oracle value. Profit scales with the depth of integrations that trust checkAMMExecutionState.

location.masks_invariant: _setReentrancyFlags(flags) from TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags strips ENTERED/NOT_ENTERED from the input flags and OR-merges with current ENTERED state. When called with NO_FLAGS (0), it produces: currentGuard & ~(ENTERED|NOT_ENTERED) | (currentGuard & ENTERED) = ENTERED. All custom flags (SWAP_GUARD_FLAG bit-2, LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG bit-7, ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG bits-7+8, FLASHLOAN_GUARD_FLAG bit-11) are cleared. This makes the guard indistinguishable from the pre-swap ENTERED state to any caller that checks specific execution flags.

hypotheses.title: Storage key asymmetry in _storeNonTokenHookFees permanently locks cross-token hook fees
hypotheses.summary: _storeNonTokenHookFees at AMMModule.sol lines 3016-3019 writes the fee storage key as efficientHash(hook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFor)) — tokenFor appears in BOTH inner positions. All read paths (_transferHookFeesByHook lines 3123-3126, getHookFeesOwedByHook) compute the key as efficientHash(hook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFee)). When tokenFee != tokenFor (cross-token hook fee payment), the write key and read key differ permanently. Fees accumulate under the wrong key and can never be withdrawn.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. A position hook (liquidity hook) or pool hook is configured to charge fees in tokenFee where tokenFee != tokenFor (e.g., protocol hook charges in USDC for ETH-related swaps). 2. During swap or liquidity operation, _storeNonTokenHookFees(hook, tokenFor, amount) at line 3016 writes: tokensOwed[hash(hook, hash(tokenFor, tokenFor))] += amount. 3. Hook operator calls collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor, tokenFee, recipient, amount). 4. _transferHookFeesByHook reads: tokensOwed[hash(hook, hash(tokenFor, tokenFee))]. 5. This key has value 0 — the fee was stored under tokenFor-tokenFor, not tokenFor-tokenFee. 6. The call fails (insufficient balance). 7. Fees stored under the wrong key are permanently inaccessible — no function exists to collect from the tokenFor-tokenFor key for cross-token scenarios.
hypotheses.victim: Hook operators whose position or pool hooks specify cross-token fee payments. Their accumulated fees are frozen in the contract with no withdrawal path. Additionally, any swapper/LP whose transaction generated these fees paid them unnecessarily.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Direct: a malicious protocol operator can advertise cross-token hook fees to attract traffic, then demonstrate the fees are unclaimable (reputation damage / insurance fraud). Indirect: attacker can use this as a griefing tool — configure cross-token fees for a victim protocol's hook to make their fee model appear broken. Fee value locked permanently scales with pool volume.

location.masks_invariant: Line 3016-3019: the inner efficientHash call uses tokenFor as BOTH arguments instead of (tokenFor, tokenFee). Token hook fees (_storeTokenHookFees) use the correct (tokenFor, tokenFee) pair. Only _storeNonTokenHookFees (called for position/pool hooks) has this bug. The asymmetry is invisible at write time because the write succeeds and emits no event with the actual key. It only manifests at read time when collection fails with balance = 0.

hypotheses.title: collectHookFeesByHook queue path has no balance validation, enabling persistent swap DoS
hypotheses.summary: collectHookFeesByHook (ModuleFeeCollection.sol:72) has no nonReentrant modifier and no balance validation in the queue path. When called during an active swap (SWAP_GUARD_FLAG set), it routes to _queueTransferHookFeesByHook which stores (hook, tokenFor, tokenFee, recipient, amount) in transient storage without checking that amount <= available hook fee balance. When swap finalization processes the queue via _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers, _transferHookFeesByHook attempts hookFeeBalance -= amount, causing underflow revert when amount > balance. This reverts the entire swap transaction.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Malicious hook MH is registered via setTokenSettings for token T. 2. A user initiates a swap through a pool containing T. 3. MH.beforeSwap (or afterSwap) callback fires. 4. Inside the callback, MH calls collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor, tokenFee, recipient, type(uint256).max). 5. SWAP_GUARD_FLAG is set -> routes to _queueTransferHookFeesByHook. No balance check performed. Queue entry written to transient storage. 6. Swap continues through pool math, output is computed. 7. _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse calls executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers. 8. _transferHookFeesByHook: hookFeeBalance[key] -= type(uint256).max -> arithmetic underflow. 9. REVERT. Entire swap transaction reverts. 10. Attack is repeatable every transaction through the pool as long as MH is registered.
hypotheses.victim: All users attempting to swap through any pool where token T has hook MH registered. Swap transactions revert at finalization after all computation — wasting user gas and preventing trading. LPs also lose fee revenue during the DoS period.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: MEV/competitive advantage: attacker blocks specific pools from trading, redirecting volume to competitor AMMs or the attacker's own pools. Extortion vector: token project extorts the protocol/LPs by threatening persistent DoS. In competitive MEV environments, eliminating arbitrage opportunities from a pool has direct dollar value.

location.masks_invariant: collectHookFeesByHook has no nonReentrant modifier (intentional — it must be callable from hook callbacks during swaps). The queue routing relies solely on SWAP_GUARD_FLAG/LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG to defer execution, not to validate the request. _queueTransferHookFeesByHook stores the raw amount without any check against tokensOwed[hookFeeKey]. The validation only happens at execution time in _transferHookFeesByHook, inside _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers, where it's too late to gracefully handle the failure.

hypotheses.title: ERC777 callback during queued fee execution re-enters collectHookFeesByHook for direct fee drain
hypotheses.summary: _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers at AMMModule.sol ~line 3190 calls _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) before the transfer loop, clearing SWAP_GUARD_FLAG and LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG while ENTERED remains set. collectHookFeesByHook (ModuleFeeCollection.sol:72) has no nonReentrant modifier — it only routes based on SWAP_GUARD_FLAG/LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG. After those flags are cleared, a reentering call to collectHookFeesByHook from an ERC777 tokensReceived callback bypasses the queue and goes directly to _transferHookFeesByHook, draining hook fee balances beyond the legitimately queued amount.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Hook H uses ERC777 token T as fee currency. T is stored in pools and used for fee payments. 2. Total hook fee balance for H = 100e18 T. H legitimately queues collection of 1e18 T during a swap. 3. Swap finalizes. _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers runs. 4. _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS): SWAP_GUARD_FLAG cleared, ENTERED remains. 5. safeTransfer(T, hookRecipient, 1e18) triggers T.tokensReceived on hookRecipient. 6. Inside tokensReceived: SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=0, ENTERED=1. Call to collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor, T, attacker, 99e18). 7. Flag check: SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=false, LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG=false, FLASHLOAN_GUARD_FLAG=false -> ELSE branch: _transferHookFeesByHook direct. 8. hookFeeBalance[key] -= 99e18 succeeds. 9. 99e18 T transferred to attacker. 10. Net: attacker receives 100e18 T (1e18 legitimate + 99e18 drained). Only 0 remaining.
hypotheses.victim: The hook fee pool — all hook operators whose accumulated fees are denominated in the ERC777 token T. The attacker drains ALL balances for that fee token across all (hook, tokenFor, tokenFee) combinations that used T.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Direct theft of accumulated hook fees. If multiple hooks have been accumulating fees in ERC777 token T, attacker drains all of them in one transaction. Profit = sum(hookFeeBalance[all_keys_for_T]) minus their legitimately queued amount.

location.masks_invariant: _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) correctly preserves ENTERED but this only protects functions with the nonReentrant modifier. collectHookFeesByHook explicitly omits nonReentrant because it must be callable from hook callbacks. Its ONLY reentrancy protection is the SWAP_GUARD_FLAG/LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG routing. After _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) clears those flags, collectHookFeesByHook loses all its reentrancy protection and any call during the transfer loop executes the direct _transferHookFeesByHook path.

hypotheses.title: createPool clears ENTERED bit via _clearReentrancyGuard before delegatecall, opening reentrant createPool window
hypotheses.summary: ModuleLiquidity.sol:79 calls _clearReentrancyGuard() which invokes _nonReentrantAfter() setting the guard to NOT_ENTERED (0x01) — clearing the ENTERED bit (0x02). The delegatecall to addLiquidity fires at line 81. Between these two lines there are no external calls in Solidity's execution model, but addLiquidity's nonReentrantWithFlags modifier re-establishes ENTERED. However, if addLiquidity's execution triggers any token hook before _nonReentrantBefore completes, the ENTERED bit is absent for a window, allowing reentrant calls to nonReentrant functions including createPool itself.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker calls createPool(detailsZ, ..., liquidityData=addLiquidity(paramsZ)). 2. _createPool runs, pool Z created. 3. _clearReentrancyGuard() at line 79: guard set to NOT_ENTERED (ENTERED=0). 4. delegatecall to addLiquidity at line 81. 5. addLiquidity's nonReentrantWithFlags(ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG) fires _nonReentrantBefore: reads NOT_ENTERED (0x01), ENTERED&0x01=0 -> OK, sets ENTERED|ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG. 6. During addLiquidity execution, a malicious token hook's beforeAddLiquidity callback fires BEFORE _nonReentrantBefore sets ENTERED. Wait -- actually _nonReentrantBefore fires first (modifier runs before function body). So the window between _clearReentrancyGuard and delegatecall is the Solidity instruction boundary -- no external calls. The real window is: outer createPool's nonReentrant after-hook sees NOT_ENTERED state if inner addLiquidity completes and then an external call happens in the gap.
hypotheses.victim: Protocol integrity — a sophisticated attacker using a malicious token hook might observe the brief NOT_ENTERED state and trigger side effects, though the practical exploitability is limited by Solidity's execution model.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Limited. The brief NOT_ENTERED window does not have any reachable external calls between lines 79 and 81 in standard execution. However, if the pool type module's createPool callback (called before line 79) or the hook validation itself has a reentrant path, a recursive createPool could succeed. Main risk: gas savings or state inconsistency if pool creation hooks fire after _clearReentrancyGuard sets NOT_ENTERED but before addLiquidity re-establishes ENTERED.

location.masks_invariant: _clearReentrancyGuard() at line 79 calls _nonReentrantAfter() which unconditionally sets the transient guard to NOT_ENTERED=0x01, clearing the ENTERED bit regardless of call depth. This is necessary to allow the delegatecall to addLiquidity (which re-checks ENTERED via its own nonReentrantWithFlags). The invariant being masked: between _clearReentrancyGuard() and addLiquidity's _nonReentrantBefore, the system has no ENTERED protection. Any external call in this micro-window could reenter without triggering the standard reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: Flash loan fee basis hijack: hook returning tokenFeeAmount > 0 computes fee on hook amount not loan amount
hypotheses.summary: In _flashLoan (AMMModule.sol lines 3302-3437), when the token hook returns tokenFeeAmount == 0, the flash loan fee is computed as loanAmount * flashLoanBPS / MAX_BPS (protocol-controlled rate). When the hook returns tokenFeeAmount > 0, the protocol treats this as the fee token amount and computes the expected repayment as tokenFeeAmount * (MAX_BPS + flashLoanBPS) / MAX_BPS. A malicious hook returning tokenFeeAmount = 1 results in a repayment requirement of approximately 1-2 wei regardless of loanAmount, enabling near-free flash loans on LP funds.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Token owner deploys MaliciousFlashHook that returns tokenFeeAmount=1 from its flash loan fee callback. 2. Token owner registers hook: setTokenSettings(token, maliciousFlashHook, PACKED_SETTINGS_WITH_FLASHLOAN_HOOK). 3. Attacker calls flashLoan(FlashloanRequest{token: tokenA, amount: 1_000_000e18, executor: exploit, data: ..., hookData: ...}). 4. _flashLoan calls hook: hook returns tokenFeeAmount=1. 5. Fee calculation path for tokenFeeAmount>0: requiredRepayment = 1 * (MAX_BPS + flashLoanBPS) / MAX_BPS ≈ 1-2 wei. 6. Attacker's executor.executeFlashloan callback receives 1_000_000e18 tokens. 7. Executor repays 1_000_000e18 + 1 wei. 8. Expected fee at 30 BPS = 1_000_000e18 * 30 / 10_000 = 3_000e18 tokens. 9. Actual fee = 1 wei. Protocol and LPs lose 3_000e18 - 1 wei in fee revenue.
hypotheses.victim: LP holders in pools containing the attacked token lose flash loan fee revenue. Protocol loses its cut of flash loan fees. Any party relying on flash loan fees as a revenue stream is impacted.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Near-free access to LP liquidity for flash loans. At 30 BPS on a $1M loan: expected fee ~$3000, actual fee ~0. Attacker can chain multiple flash loans in a single transaction. MEV bots with access to LP liquidity for arbitrage via flash loans gain competitive advantage worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per day on high-volume tokens.

location.masks_invariant: The flash loan fee computation has a conditional branch: if tokenFeeAmount==0, use loanAmount as basis; if tokenFeeAmount>0, use tokenFeeAmount as basis. The hook can freely return any value for tokenFeeAmount. Since token owners control their hooks via setTokenSettings, they can install a hook that returns tokenFeeAmount=1 for ALL flash loans of their token, reducing protocol flash loan fees to zero. The protocol's flashLoanBPS setting is effectively overrideable by token owners.

hypotheses.title: Malicious hook LP lock: queue poisoning via hook callbacks prevents removeLiquidity, trapping LP funds
hypotheses.summary: A token owner installs a malicious hook that calls collectHookFeesByHook with amount > available balance during every liquidity operation callback. Since LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG is set during addLiquidity/removeLiquidity, these calls queue the poisoned amount. When the operation finalizes and processes the queue via _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers, underflow revert aborts the entire transaction. This makes it impossible for LPs to call removeLiquidity for pools containing the malicious token — permanently locking LP funds.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker creates token T and deploys MaliciousHook MH. 2. MH's beforeRemoveLiquidity (or afterAddLiquidity) callback calls collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor, tokenFee, attacker, type(uint256).max). 3. Token owner registers MH via setTokenSettings(T, MH, PACKED_SETTINGS). 4. Attacker attracts LPs to deposit into a T-containing pool (offering high fee incentives). 5. When LPs attempt removeLiquidity, LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG is set. 6. MH.beforeRemoveLiquidity fires -> collectHookFeesByHook queues type(uint256).max. 7. removeLiquidity finalizes -> _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers -> underflow revert. 8. Every removeLiquidity attempt for this pool reverts. 9. LP funds permanently locked (addLiquidity may also be poisoned to prevent partial recovery). 10. Token owner extracted value from the pool before enabling the lock.
hypotheses.victim: LP holders who deposited into pools containing token T. Their deposited funds (both token T and the paired token) are permanently locked — they cannot call removeLiquidity or collectFees.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Rug pull variant: attacker attracts LP deposits, then poisons the pool. Attacker has previously withdrawn their own liquidity or can call removeLiquidity before activating the poison hook. LP victims permanently lose access to their deposited funds. For a pool with $1M TVL, attacker extracts that full value indirectly (through price manipulation, directional bets funded by the locked funds, or if they hold the token they benefit from forced token demand).

location.masks_invariant: collectHookFeesByHook routes to the queue whenever LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG is set (bit 7). This flag is set by ALL liquidity operations: addLiquidity uses ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG=384 which includes bit 7, removeLiquidity uses REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG which also includes bit 7, and collectFees uses COLLECT_FEES_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG. Therefore, any hook callback fired during ANY liquidity operation can poison the queue with an unbounded amount. Since no balance check exists at queue time, and _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers is called at the end of every liquidity operation, every liquidity operation for a poisoned pool will revert.

hypotheses.title: Flag non-overlap: singleSwap callable during addLiquidity hook — stale-reserve price manipulation
hypotheses.summary: nonReentrantWithFlags uses bitwise overlap check: if (incomingFlags & currentFlags != 0) revert. ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x180 (bits 7+8). SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG = 0x1C (bits 2+3+4). Bitwise AND = 0. Therefore singleSwap is callable during any addLiquidity hook callback. This is NOT gated by setTokenSettings — the liquidity hook is set per-position by the LP calling addLiquidity. A malicious LP sets themselves as liquidityHook for their own position and re-enters singleSwap within the hook. At hook fire time, pool reserves are stale (updated AFTER _executeAddLiquidityHooks in _positionAddLiquidity at line ~470), enabling the swap to execute against pre-deposit price.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker is an LP. They call addLiquidity with liquidityHooksExtraData.liquidityHook = address(MaliciousLiquidityHook). 2. _positionAddLiquidity calls pool type addLiquidity at line ~411, updating pool type's internal state. 3. _executeAddLiquidityHooks at line ~463 calls MaliciousLiquidityHook.afterAddLiquidity. 4. At this point: pool type has post-deposit liquidity, but LimitBreakAMM reserves still show pre-deposit values (ptrPoolState.reserve0 += deposit0 at line ~470 has NOT run). 5. Attacker calls singleSwap(SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG). 6. nonReentrantWithFlags check: 0x1C & 0x180 = 0 → PASS. 7. Swap executes against pool type that now has extra liquidity (attacker's deposit). 8. LimitBreakAMM reads stale reserves for any accounting. 9. Attacker's deposit artificially moves the price in the pool type while accounting shows pre-deposit price. 10. Attacker extracts value from the delta.
hypotheses.victim: Other LPs in the target pool whose positions are priced against the manipulated post-deposit pool type state. MEV arbitrageurs lose their fair arbitrage opportunity as the attacker front-runs the price correction.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker adds large liquidity at Step 1, moving the price. The hook-triggered singleSwap at Step 6 captures the arbitrage on the price movement introduced by the attacker's own deposit. After collecting the swap profit, attacker removes liquidity. Net: zero-cost price manipulation and arbitrage capture in one transaction.

location.masks_invariant: ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x180) = bit7 | bit8. SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (0x1C) = bit2 | bit3 | bit4. These share zero bits. MULTI_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (0x2C) = bit2 | bit3 | bit5, also zero overlap. DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (0x44) = bit2 | bit6, also zero overlap. All swap variants are callable during addLiquidity hook. Reserve update at line ~470 is AFTER hook execution, creating a stale-reserve window for the entire swap nested within the hook.

hypotheses.title: Flag non-overlap: removeLiquidity callable during singleSwap token hook — LP drain before swap settlement
hypotheses.summary: SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG = 0x1C. REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x280 (bits 7+9). AND = 0. During singleSwap execution, token hooks (ILimitBreakAMMTokenHook with BEFORE_SWAP or AFTER_SWAP flag) fire while the swap is in progress. At the after-swap hook point (AMMModule.sol line ~1445), the pool type has committed the swap output but LimitBreakAMM's _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse (line ~2144) has not yet run. An attacker who owns a token (can call setTokenSettings) installs a hook that calls removeLiquidity from within the after-swap callback, draining LP reserves before the swap's fund collection finalizes. This is a complete LP rug in a single transaction.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker owns token T. Deploys MaliciousTokenHook (MTH) with AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set. 2. amm.setTokenSettings(T, MTH, PACKED_SETTINGS). Requires token ownership. 3. Victim LPs deposit into pool P (T / stablecoin). 4. Attacker adds own liquidity to pool P to establish LP position. 5. Attacker initiates singleSwap through pool P. 6. After pool type swap committed at line ~1435-1442, MTH.afterSwap fires at line ~1445. 7. REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x280) & SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (0x1C) = 0 → removeLiquidity guard passes. 8. MTH calls amm.removeLiquidity() — attacker removes their LP position. 9. ptrPoolState.reserve0 -= withdraw0 executes inside the hook. 10. Swap's _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse at line ~2144 now tries to collect swap input from pools with depleted reserves. 11. If pool type had T as output token, stablecoin reserves may be insufficient. 12. At minimum: attacker performs a zero-slippage LP exit during peak price impact of their own swap.
hypotheses.victim: LPs in any pool containing token T. Token owner can drain LP positions at will. Every user who provides liquidity to a pool with a malicious token is a potential victim.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Full LP drain: attacker adds LP, swaps (moving price), then removes LP atomically during the swap hook. The swap's price impact is borne by OTHER LPs (impermanent loss), while attacker exits at the pre-swap price. Repeated over many blocks: consistent, risk-free LP extraction. For a $1M TVL pool: attacker captures near 100% of the pool's value over time.

location.masks_invariant: SINGLE_POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG (0x1C) vs REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x280): AND=0. Also: REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG & ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x180) = 0x80 (bit7 shared) → remove cannot reenter during add. But REMOVE vs SINGLE_POOL_SWAP=0, REMOVE vs MULTI_POOL_SWAP (0x2C)=0, REMOVE vs DIRECT_SWAP (0x44)=0. All swap types allow remove reentrancy. The after-swap hook fires BEFORE _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse, which means LP reserves can be drained before the swap's token movements are reconciled.

hypotheses.title: Hook fee double-claiming: HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG token hook doubles as pool hook, collapsing two distinct fee slots into one claimable key
hypotheses.summary: AMMModule._storeHookFees (lines 2978-2982) — for TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG tokens — writes fees at key efficientHash(tokenForSettings.tokenHook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFee)). AMMModule._storeNonTokenHookFees (lines 3016-3019) writes fees at key efficientHash(hook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFor)). When the SAME contract address H is registered as tokenHook for token T with HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG AND is also passed as the poolHook (or liquidityHook) for a pool containing T, swap-path fees (via _storeHookFees with tokenFee=T) and liquidity-path fees (via _storeNonTokenHookFees with tokenFor=T) both resolve to efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T, T)). H calling collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor=T, tokenFee=T, ...) claims BOTH sources simultaneously, receiving fees that were intended to be independently tracked.
hypotheses.mechanism: 1. Attacker deploys contract H. 2. Token owner registers H as tokenHook for token T: setTokenSettings(T, H, TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG | TOKEN_SETTINGS_BEFORE_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG). 3. Attacker creates pool T/USDC using H as poolHook. 4. Victim LP adds liquidity to pool T/USDC. _positionAddLiquidity fires _executePoolModifyLiquidityHook, which calls H.validatePoolAddLiquidity. H returns hookFee0=X. 5. _storeNonTokenHookFees(H, T, X) writes at key K = efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T, T)). 6. Victim swaps T→USDC through the pool. H.beforeSwap fires, returning tokenInHookFee=Y. 7. _applySwapByInputInputFees calls _storeHookFees(T, T, tokenTSettings, Y). Since TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG is set, writes at key K2 = efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T, T)) — SAME key K. 8. tokensOwed[K] = X + Y. 9. H calls collectHookFeesByHook(T, T, recipient, X+Y) and collects BOTH the LP-operation fee (X) intended for the pool hook role AND the swap fee (Y) intended for the token hook role. These were meant to be independently tracked and potentially independently rate-limited.
hypotheses.victim: LPs and protocol revenue: if the intended design was for pool hook fees (X) and token swap hook fees (Y) to be tracked separately (e.g., different rate limits, different recipients within H's internal accounting), the collision allows H to drain both simultaneously. Additionally, if there was supposed to be a separate fee recipient for pool-hook fees vs. token-hook fees (different sub-addresses within a hook system), that distinction is lost.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: An attacker who controls both the tokenHook registration and the poolHook registration can accumulate fees from BOTH swap activity and liquidity activity in a single claimable slot, then sweep the combined balance in one transaction. At high pool volumes, this is the difference between claiming swap fees only (~0.1% * volume) vs. swap fees + liquidity hook fees (~0.1% * volume + 0.X% * TVL). On a $10M TVL pool with $1M daily volume: token swap hook fees ≈ $100/day, liquidity hook fees ≈ $100-500/day. Combined double-claim possible when they share a key.

location.masks_invariant: _storeHookFees (HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG branch): key = efficientHash(tokenForSettings.tokenHook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFee)). When tokenFee==tokenFor==T and tokenHook==H, key = efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T, T)). _storeNonTokenHookFees: key = efficientHash(hook, efficientHash(tokenFor, tokenFor)). When hook==H, tokenFor==T, key = efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T, T)). Identical. No runtime check prevents H from being simultaneously a token hook (with HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG) and a pool/liquidity hook. The protocol implicitly assumes these two roles have distinct identities.

coupled_pair.state_a: tokensOwed[efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T,T))] written by _storeHookFees when TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG set and tokenFee==tokenFor
coupled_pair.state_b: tokensOwed[efficientHash(H, efficientHash(T,T))] written by _storeNonTokenHookFees when hook==H and tokenFor==T
coupled_pair.invariant: Fees accumulated via token-hook swap path and fees accumulated via pool/liquidity-hook path for the same hook H should be distinguishable and independently claimable; they must NOT share a storage slot

hypotheses.title: Flag non-overlap: addLiquidity callable during removeLiquidity hook — reserve manipulation grief/exploit
hypotheses.summary: REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x280 (bits 7+9). ADD_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x180 (bits 7+8). Bitwise AND = 0x80 (bit 7, LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG shared). Wait — 0x280 & 0x180 = 0x80 ≠ 0, so direct add-during-remove is BLOCKED. However: REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x280) & COLLECT_FEES_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (0x480) = 0x80 ≠ 0 also blocked. CORRECTION: The primary non-overlap is swap ↔ liquidity, not liquidity ↔ liquidity. This hypothesis covers the COLLECT_FEES path during removeLiquidity hooks: COLLECT_FEES_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x480, REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG = 0x280. 0x480 & 0x280 = 0x80 → overlap on bit7 → BLOCKED. Downgrade: the cross-liquidity reentrancy is mitigated by shared bit7. The critical vectors are swap↔liquidity non-overlaps covered in H-08 and H-09.
hypotheses.mechanism: REVISED: This hypothesis confirms the SWAP vs LIQUIDITY flag non-overlap as the primary attack surface. Liquidity-vs-liquidity operations share LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG (bit7=0x80) and are therefore mutually blocked. Only swap operations (SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=bit2) are orthogonal to liquidity operations (LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG=bit7). The distinct guard hierarchy means: any swap can execute during any liquidity hook and vice versa. This extends to: (a) singleSwap during addLiquidity hook [H-08], (b) removeLiquidity during singleSwap token hook [H-09], (c) addLiquidity during singleSwap token hook, (d) collectFees during singleSwap token hook. Attack (d): attacker's token hook during singleSwap calls collectFees on a position, capturing fee growth before the position's fee growth is properly updated post-swap.
hypotheses.victim: LPs whose fee growth is captured by an attacker calling collectFees from within a singleSwap token hook, before the swap's fee distribution updates the position's fee growth globals.
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker who controls a token hook can call collectFees on victim LP positions during a swap hook, capturing their pending fees at a fee-growth snapshot from before the swap increments globals. Depending on pool fee accrual speed: moderate value capture per transaction.

location.masks_invariant: Guard flag hierarchy: SWAP base (bit2) ← POOL_SWAP (bits2+3) ← SINGLE_POOL_SWAP (bits2+3+4), MULTI_POOL_SWAP (bits2+3+5), DIRECT_SWAP (bits2+6). LIQUIDITY base (bit7) ← ADD_LIQUIDITY (bits7+8), REMOVE_LIQUIDITY (bits7+9), COLLECT_FEES (bits7+10). FLASHLOAN (bit11). The two trees (SWAP and LIQUIDITY) share no bits. The guard check `_isReentrancyFlagSet(incomingFlags)` only passes if ALL bits of incomingFlags are already set in current flags. Entering any SWAP operation while in a LIQUIDITY hook succeeds because the SWAP flag bits (bit2 etc) are never set by LIQUIDITY guard. This architectural decision is the root cause of H-08, H-09, and this hypothesis.
